name: Great cerebral vein and deep venous system
summary: The deep structures drain through a system of veins that converge on the great cerebral vein of Galen beneath the splenium. The internal cerebral veins form at the foramen of Monro from the thalamostriate and septal veins, run back in the roof of the third ventricle (velum interpositum) and unite as the vein of Galen, which is joined by the basal veins of Rosenthal (draining the insula, medial temporal lobe and midbrain) and empties into the straight sinus. Thrombosis of this system produces bilateral thalamic infarction, and vein of Galen malformations in infants cause heart failure and hydrocephalus.

anatomy.location: Internal cerebral veins in the velum interpositum above the third ventricle, curving around the pulvinar; vein of Galen in the quadrigeminal cistern below the splenium, ending at the anterior end of the straight sinus; basal veins around the midbrain in the ambient cisterns.

paired internal cerebral veins in the roof of the third ventricle

imaging.normalAppearance: Paired flow voids in the roof of the third ventricle on axial T2 and a short midline vessel beneath the splenium on sagittal images; on venography the deep system is a constant landmark. Loss of flow with bilateral thalamic edema is deep venous thrombosis; a giant midline venous pouch in an infant is a vein of Galen malformation.

pathology.finding: Absent flow in the internal cerebral veins and vein of Galen with bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia edema and hemorrhage.
Massively dilated midline venous pouch fed by choroidal arteries in a neonate with heart failure and hydrocephalus.

pathology.pathology: Pineal region tumor displacing the deep veins
pathology.finding: Mass elevating the internal cerebral veins and compressing the vein of Galen.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: MR venography with T1 and SWI; cardiac assessment in neonates

lesionEffects.deficit: Coma, bilateral thalamic dysfunction, vertical gaze palsy
Hydrocephalus and heart failure in infancy
lesionEffects.mechanism: Vein of Galen malformation compressing the aqueduct and shunting cardiac output

pearls: The internal cerebral veins mark the roof of the third ventricle: a mass that displaces them is pineal or thalamic
